Control Inversion (IOC) explained in a simple and practical way

The video explains the inversion of control (IOC): the component stops creating its own dependencies and starts receiving them from outside. It shows the injection of dependency via builder, the use of mocks in tests and IoC containers that assemble dependencies in large systems.

Published in 23 January 2026 · 5 min 57 s

  • Specification and development

Open on YouTube

The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets lead to the stretch of the video.

The problem: strong coupling

According to the video, a small change in code breaks another part that was unrelated to it, and writing a simple test becomes a problem because the code depends on the database or a cloud service 00:23.

The cause is usually in one line: the class ClientHandler creates its own dependence, the ClientRepository. That's strong coupling: the two classes get stuck to each other, and changing one tends to break the other 00:46.

What is control inversion

The control inversion (IoC) reverses who is in charge: instead of the component creating what it needs, it delegates this responsibility to someone from outside, like a framework 01:06.

The video uses the Hollywood principle: the actor does not call the studio asking if there is paper; he leaves contact, and the studio calls when the time comes. Likewise, the components do not seek the dependencies; they expect the environment to deliver them. 01:27.

Dependency injection

The main way to apply IoC is to inject dependence: the component stops creating dependencies and receives them ready, from outside 01:49.

In the video example, dependency becomes a constructor parameter. Class ClientHandler Just declare what you need and expect someone to deliver 02:10.

The injection via builder is the most common way and has three steps 02:32:

1. The class declares in the builder everything it needs 02:32. 2. Someone outside creates these dependencies 02:53. 3. When creating the class, these dependencies are delivered to it 02:53.

The Gain: Testability

The main benefit is the testability, and it leads to the concept of mock 03:15.

A mock is like a movie stunt: a fake object that simulates a real dependency, such as access to the database, in a way that the test completely controls 03:37.

Like the ClientHandler receives the repository from outside, the test delivers a fake repository that pretends to find the client. Thus, class logic is tested isolated, without real database 03:58.

Easier code to maintain and evolve

According to the video, the result is a more robust code, because each part can be tested separately, and easier to maintain, because the dependencies become explicit 04:20.

It also makes it easier to evolve: you can trade an SQL bank for a NoSQL without touching the classes that use it. The code exits the strong coupling, with glued parts, for the weak coupling, with parts that fit as Lego 04:41.

Containers of IoC

In large systems, no one gives that injection by hand, class by class. For this there are containers of IoC, or injection of dependence 05:02.

The video compares the container to a master of works: it reads the application plant, sees that the class A needs B and B needs C, and she rides it all alone. 05:23.

The video closes with a paradox: when components give up control of dependencies, those who develop gain power to test, modify and evolve the system. Control inversion does not take control; it puts control in the right place 05:45.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between inversion of control and injection of dependency?

Inversion of control is the principle: the component does not create its own dependencies. Addiction injection is the main way to apply this principle 01:49.

Why does IoC facilitate testing?

Because the class gets dependency from outside, and the test can deliver a mock instead of real dependency 03:58.
